Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

Assume the axiom of choice so that the library's conditional-expectation
classes are available. Let $Y$ and $Z$ be random elements and let
$\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be a sigma-algebra. We say that $Y$ and $Z$ are
**conditionally independent given $\mathcal G$**, and write
$Y\perp\!\!\!\perp Z\mid\mathcal G$, if for every pair of bounded measurable
real functions $f,g$,
$$ \mathbb E[f(Y)g(Z)\mid\mathcal G] =\mathbb E[f(Y)\mid\mathcal G]\, \mathbb E[g(Z)\mid\mathcal G]\quad\text{a.s.} $$
This is an equality of almost-everywhere classes and hence does not depend on
representatives.

For sigma-algebras $\mathcal H_1,\mathcal H_2\subseteq\mathcal F$, the notation
$\mathcal H_1\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal H_2\mid\mathcal G$ means the same identity
for every bounded $\mathcal H_1$-measurable $U$ and bounded
$\mathcal H_2$-measurable $V$.

The definition is symmetric. If $\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$ modulo
null sets, it reduces to ordinary independence. If one side is
$\mathcal G$-measurable, conditional independence is automatic because that
factor is already known when conditioning. The choices of the zero function or
the constant-one function cause no exceptional case.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$

  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: The state space $\{0,1\}^m\times\{0,1\}^n$ has $2^{m+n}$ elements. Every term $\exp(-E(v,h))$ is finite and positive, so their finite sum $Z$ is finite and positive; therefore $p$ is a probability mass function.

For fixed $v$, put $c_j=b_j+(W^Tv)_j$. Then $\exp(-E(v,h))=\exp(a^Tv)\prod_j\exp(h_jc_j)$, and summing over binary $h$ gives $\exp(a^Tv)\prod_j(1+\exp(c_j))$. Thus $p(h\mid v)$ is the product of Bernoulli masses with success probabilities $\exp(c_j)/(1+\exp(c_j))=\sigma(c_j)$.

For fixed $h$, put $d_i=a_i+(Wh)_i$. Then $\exp(-E(v,h))=\exp(b^Th)\prod_i\exp(v_id_i)$, and summing over binary $v$ gives $\exp(b^Th)\prod_i(1+\exp(d_i))$. Hence $p(v\mid h)$ is the product of Bernoulli masses with success probabilities $\exp(d_i)/(1+\exp(d_i))=\sigma(d_i)$.

The product conditional mass functions in steps 1.2–1.3 make the conditional expectations of any bounded measurable functions of disjoint coordinates factor into the product of their conditional expectations. By [F1]–[F2], each layer is therefore conditionally independent given the other in the stated sigma-algebra sense. This use of the conditional-expectation convention is the only proof point needing [A1].

For fixed observed $v$, $p(v)=Z^{-1}\exp(a^Tv)\sum_h\exp(b^Th+v^TWh)$. Differentiating these finite sums gives $\partial_{W_{ij}}\log p(v)=v_i\mathbb E_{p(h\mid v)}[h_j]-\partial_{W_{ij}}\log Z$; the same calculation gives $\partial_{a_i}\log p(v)=v_i-\partial_{a_i}\log Z$ and $\partial_{b_j}\log p(v)=\mathbb E_{p(h\mid v)}[h_j]-\partial_{b_j}\log Z$.

Differentiating the finite partition sum yields $\partial_{W_{ij}}\log Z=\sum_{v',h'}v_i'h_j'p(v',h')=\mathbb E_p[V_iH_j]$, $\partial_{a_i}\log Z=\mathbb E_p[V_i]$, and $\partial_{b_j}\log Z=\mathbb E_p[H_j]$. Substitution in step 2.1 gives the exact gradients in the Definition.

For each visible state $v$, $\sum_{v'}K(v,v')=\sum_h p(h\mid v)\sum_{v'}p(v'\mid h)=\sum_hp(h\mid v)=1$. Thus K is a stochastic matrix and each $q_k^v$ is a well-defined finite probability distribution. Replacing the exact negative-phase marginal $p(v')$ in the gradient formulas by $q_k^v(v')$ gives the finite contrastive-divergence statistic defined in the Statement.

citations.quote: For $N,p\ge1$ and data $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in\mathbb R^p$, put $\bar x=N^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^N x_r$ and $S=N^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^N(x_r-\bar x)(x_r-\bar x)^T$. For any symmetric positive-semidefinite $S$ and any $\Theta\in\mathbb S_{++}^p$, set $\ell_S(\Theta)=\log\det\Theta-\operatorname{tr}(S\Theta)$, where $\mathbb S_{++}^p$ is the cone of symmetric positive-definite $p\times p$ matrices. Define $\|\Theta\|_1=\sum_{i=1}^p\sum_{j=1}^p|\Theta_{ij}|$, including diagonal entries, and for $\lambda>0$ define $F_{S,\lambda}(\Theta)=\ell_S(\Theta)-\lambda\|\Theta\|_1$. The off-diagonal-only convention $F^{\mathrm{off}}_{S,\lambda}(\Theta)=\ell_S(\Theta)-\lambda\sum_{i\ne j}|\Theta_{ij}|$ is a separate objective.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

derivations.claim: For any nonzero $x\in\mathbb R^p$, $x^TWx=x^TSx+\lambda\|x\|^2\ge\lambda\|x\|^2>0$, so the initialized $W$ is symmetric positive definite.

Suppose the current $W$ is positive definite. Its principal submatrix $V$ is positive definite, so $V_{\ell\ell}>0$ for each coordinate. With other coordinates fixed, the lasso objective $\tfrac12\beta^TV\beta-s^T\beta+\lambda\|\beta\|_1$ as a function of $\beta_\ell=t$ is $\tfrac12V_{\ell\ell}t^2-rt+\lambda|t|+\text{constant}$, where $r=s_\ell-\sum_{k\ne\ell}V_{\ell k}\beta_k$. Its unique minimizer is $(r-\lambda)/V_{\ell\ell}$ when $r>\lambda$, zero when $|r|\le\lambda$, and $(r+\lambda)/V_{\ell\ell}$ when $r<-\lambda$, exactly the displayed soft-threshold update. Hence every finite coordinate sweep is well-defined.

Each block candidate is a finite symmetric matrix. By [F2] it has a symmetric eigendecomposition, and all its eigenvalues are positive exactly when it is positive definite. The procedure accepts only candidates passing this finite test, so positive definiteness is invariant until either an explicit failure is returned or all $Rp$ blocks finish.

The fixed positive integers $R$ and $K$ bound all outer and inner loops, so the procedure terminates. On success the final $W$ is positive definite by step 2.1, hence $W^{-1}$ exists and is positive definite. The procedure makes no conclusion that this truncated output maximizes $F_{S,\lambda}$ or that increasing $R$ and $K$ converges.

$$m(y)=\int_E p(x,y)\,\mu(dx),\qquad D=\{y:0<m(y)<\infty\},$$
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_Ap(x,y)\,\mu(dx)}{m(y)},&y\in D,\\ \rho(A),&y\notin D.\end{cases}$$

$Y\perp\!\!\!\perp Z\mid\mathcal G$, if for every pair of bounded measurable
real functions $f,g$,

This is an equality of almost-everywhere classes and hence does not depend on
representatives.

for every bounded $\mathcal H_1$-measurable $U$ and bounded
$\mathcal H_2$-measurable $V$.

null sets, it reduces to ordinary independence. If one side is
$\mathcal G$-measurable, conditional independence is automatic because that
factor is already known when conditioning. The choices of the zero function or

> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

A clique is a nonempty subset $C\subseteq V$ whose distinct vertices are adjacent. derivations.claim: Fix distinct $i,j$. By [A1], [F1] and [F2], the joint density of $X$ is the stated nondegenerate Gaussian density; here positive definiteness is an additional hypothesis beyond the singular-covariance multivariate-normal definition.

In the correspondingly permuted precision matrix write $\Theta=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\B^T&C\end{pmatrix}$, where $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&c\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$. For every nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^2$, $u^TAu=(u,0)^T\Theta(u,0)>0$, so $A$ is positive definite and $\det A=ad-c^2>0$. If $p=2$, the $Z$ coordinate is a singleton and the following conditional-density calculation is the unconditional bivariate density.

For $p>2$, [F7] supplies the countable-choice hypothesis of [F6], so the joint Euclidean density in [F2] is also a density relative to $\lambda_2\otimes\lambda_{p-2}$. Put $u=y-\mu_Y$, $w=z-\mu_Z$, and $D=C-B^TA^{-1}B$. For nonzero $w$, $(-A^{-1}Bw,w)^T\Theta(-A^{-1}Bw,w)=w^TDw>0$, hence $D$ is positive definite. Completing the square gives $u^TAu+2u^TBw+w^TCw=(u+A^{-1}Bw)^TA(u+A^{-1}Bw)+w^TDw$. The section integral over $y$ is therefore positive and finite for every $z$: its $y$ factor is the normalized two-dimensional Gaussian density with precision $A$, multiplied by a finite positive constant.

For $p>2$, use the explicit filler probability concentrated at $(0,0)$ on $\mathbb R^2$ in [F3]; the positive finite marginal sections from step 3.1 show that the conditional law at every $z$ has density $\frac{\sqrt{\det A}}{2\pi}\exp(-\tfrac12(u+A^{-1}Bw)^TA(u+A^{-1}Bw))$. It is the bivariate normal law with mean $\mu_Y-A^{-1}B(z-\mu_Z)$ and covariance $A^{-1}$. For $p=2$, this is the unconditional law with covariance $\Theta^{-1}=A^{-1}$.

If $\Theta_{ij}=c=0$, then $A$ is diagonal and the conditional density in step 4.1 is a product of two univariate Gaussian densities for every $z$. Its conditional expectations therefore factor for all bounded measurable coordinate functions; [F4] gives $X_i\perp\!\!\!\perp X_j\mid\sigma(Z)$.

Conversely, suppose $X_i\perp\!\!\!\perp X_j\mid\sigma(Z)$. Apply [F4] to the four bounded pairs formed from $\cos(X_i),\sin(X_i)$ and $\cos(X_j),\sin(X_j)$ and combine the resulting identities. For almost every $z$, the conditional joint characteristic function at $(1,1)$ equals the product of its conditional marginal characteristic functions. By [F1], [F4] and [F5], the joint characteristic function from step 4.1 is $\exp(i(m_1(z)+m_2(z))-\tfrac12((A^{-1})_{11}+2(A^{-1})_{12}+(A^{-1})_{22}))$, whereas that product omits the middle covariance term. Equality implies $\exp(-(A^{-1})_{12})=1$, and since $(A^{-1})_{12}$ is real this forces $(A^{-1})_{12}=0$.

The inverse of $A$ is $(ad-c^2)^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}d&-c\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}$. Since $\det A>0$, $(A^{-1})_{12}=0$ if and only if $c=0$, which is exactly $\Theta_{ij}=0$. citations.quote: For $N,p\ge1$ and data $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in\mathbb R^p$, put $\bar x=N^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^N x_r$ and $S=N^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^N(x_r-\bar x)(x_r-\bar x)^T$. For any symmetric positive-semidefinite $S$ and any $\Theta\in\mathbb S_{++}^p$, set $\ell_S(\Theta)=\log\det\Theta-\operatorname{tr}(S\Theta)$, where $\mathbb S_{++}^p$ is the cone of symmetric positive-definite $p\times p$ matrices. Define $\|\Theta\|_1=\sum_{i=1}^p\sum_{j=1}^p|\Theta_{ij}|$, including diagonal entries, and for $\lambda>0$ define $F_{S,\lambda}(\Theta)=\ell_S(\Theta)-\lambda\|\Theta\|_1$. The off-diagonal-only convention $F^{\mathrm{off}}_{S,\lambda}(\Theta)=\ell_S(\Theta)-\lambda\sum_{i\ne j}|\Theta_{ij}|$ is a separate objective.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The following are equivalent:

1. $T$ is non-negative.
2. $T$ is self-adjoint and every eigenvalue of $T$ is a nonnegative real number.
3. Some orthonormal basis makes the matrix of $T$ diagonal with nonnegative real diagonal entries.
4. There exists a linear map $S:V\to V$ such that $T=S^*S$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

A $C^2$ function on an open convex set is convex if and only if its Hessian is positive semidefinite at every point. Hessians and their quadratic forms have the conventions of [[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]], [[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]].

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be convex ([[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]). The function $f:C\to\mathbb R$ is convex when $f((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)$ for all $x,y\in C$ and $t\in[0,1]$. The parameter interval is the closed interval of [[def-interval]].

It is strictly convex when the inequality is strict for distinct $x,y$ and $0<t<1$. No strict inequality is required at $t=0$ or $t=1$, where the two sides coincide. The empty set and a singleton support convex functions, and strict convexity on either is vacuous.

derivations.claim: By the all-entry objective definition [F1] and the nonnegative-operator factorization [F2], write $S=R^TR$. Thus $\operatorname{tr}(S\Theta)=\operatorname{tr}(R\Theta R^T)\ge0$ for $\Theta\succ0$. Also $\|\Theta\|_1=\sum_{i,j}|\Theta_{ij}|\ge\sum_i\Theta_{ii}=\operatorname{tr}\Theta$, since positive-definite matrices have positive diagonal entries.

By [F3], the eigenvalues $t_1,\ldots,t_p$ of $\Theta\succ0$ are positive and $\log\det\Theta=\sum_k\log t_k$, $\operatorname{tr}\Theta=\sum_k t_k$. Hence $F_{S,\lambda}(\Theta)\le\sum_{k=1}^p h(t_k)$ for $h(t)=\log t-\lambda t$. The function $h$ is bounded above and tends to $-\infty$ as $t\downarrow0$ or $t\to\infty$. For any $c$, the upper level set $F_{S,\lambda}(\Theta)\ge c$ therefore forces each eigenvalue into a compact interval $[a_c,b_c]\subset(0,\infty)$: if $M=\sup_{t>0}h(t)$, then each $h(t_k)\ge c-(p-1)M$. These matrices form a closed bounded set of symmetric matrices contained in $\mathbb S_{++}^p$, hence a compact set. Taking $c=F_{S,\lambda}(I)$ gives a nonempty compact upper level set, and continuity of $F$ yields a maximizer.

The cone $\mathbb S_{++}^p$ is open and convex: positive quadratic forms remain positive under sufficiently small symmetric perturbations, and convex combinations of positive quadratic forms remain positive. For symmetric $H$, determinant expansion gives $\left.\frac{d}{dt}\log\det(\Theta+tH)\right|_{t=0}=\operatorname{tr}(\Theta^{-1}H)$. Differentiating $(\Theta+tH)(\Theta+tH)^{-1}=I$ gives $\left.\frac{d}{dt}(\Theta+tH)^{-1}\right|_{t=0}=-\Theta^{-1}H\Theta^{-1}$, so the second directional derivative is $-\operatorname{tr}(\Theta^{-1}H\Theta^{-1}H)$.

Let $B=\Theta^{-1/2}H\Theta^{-1/2}$, using the positive square root from the orthonormal eigenbasis [F3]. Then $B$ is symmetric and $\operatorname{tr}(\Theta^{-1}H\Theta^{-1}H)=\operatorname{tr}(B^2)=\|B\|_F^2$, strictly positive when $H\ne0$. Thus the second derivative of $\log\det$ along every nonconstant segment is strictly negative, giving its strict chord inequality. The Hessian of $-\log\det$ is positive semidefinite by step 2.1, so [F4] gives convexity in the chord sense of [F5]. The trace term is linear and the entrywise $\ell^1$ norm is convex by the triangle inequality, so its negative is concave; adding these terms preserves the strict chord inequality. Hence $F_{S,\lambda}$ is strictly concave on its open convex domain.

Put $G=\Theta^{-1}-S$. At a maximizer every feasible one-coordinate directional derivative is at most zero, and when the objective is differentiable in both directions its derivative is zero. Since $\Theta_{ii}>0$, the diagonal penalty is locally differentiable with slope $1$, so the diagonal equation is $G_{ii}-\lambda=0$ and $\Gamma_{ii}=1$. For $i<j$, a symmetric perturbation by $t(E_{ij}+E_{ji})$ has smooth derivative $2G_{ij}t$ and changes the penalty by $2\lambda(|\Theta_{ij}+t|-|\Theta_{ij}|)$. If $\Theta_{ij}\ne0$, testing both signs of small $t$ gives $G_{ij}=\lambda\operatorname{sign}(\Theta_{ij})$. If $\Theta_{ij}=0$, taking $t>0$ gives $G_{ij}\le\lambda$ and taking $t<0$ gives $G_{ij}\ge-\lambda$. Defining $\Gamma_{ij}=\Gamma_{ji}=G_{ij}/\lambda$ at zero and the sign otherwise yields the stated KKT equation for the all-entry penalty [F1].

Conversely, suppose $\Theta\succ0$ and a symmetric $\Gamma$ satisfies the stated entrywise conditions and $\Theta^{-1}-S-\lambda\Gamma=0$. Put $T=\Theta^{-1/2}\Theta'\Theta^{-1/2}$ for any $\Theta'\succ0$; its eigenvalues $t_r$ are positive. Since $\log t\le t-1$ for $t>0$ (the function $t-1-\log t$ has its minimum $0$ at $t=1$), $\log\det\Theta'-\log\det\Theta=\sum_r\log t_r\le\operatorname{tr}(T)-p=\operatorname{tr}(\Theta^{-1}(\Theta'-\Theta))$. For each scalar $x$ and each allowed subgradient $\gamma$ of $|x|$, $|y|\ge|x|+\gamma(y-x)$: if $x\ne0$, this follows from $|y|\ge\operatorname{sign}(x)y$, while for $x=0$ it follows from $|\gamma|\le1$. Summing gives $\|\Theta'\|_1\ge\|\Theta\|_1+\sum_{i,j}\Gamma_{ij}(\Theta'_{ij}-\Theta_{ij})$ for the all-entry objective [F1]. Combining these bounds with the linear trace term and the KKT equation yields $F_{S,\lambda}(\Theta')-F_{S,\lambda}(\Theta)\le\operatorname{tr}((\Theta^{-1}-S-\lambda\Gamma)(\Theta'-\Theta))=0$. Thus every such KKT point is a maximizer. The maximizer exists by step 1.2 and is unique by strict concavity from step 2.2, so the KKT condition is both necessary and sufficient for that unique optimum.

Thus the intercept and $S$ design has rank $s+1$ almost surely. Conditional on that design, an orthonormal basis of its orthogonal complement has dimension $m=n-|S|-1$. In that basis the projected residual pairs are $m$ independent copies of this Gaussian residual; standardizing the two coordinates does not change their sample correlation. Thus the sample partial correlation has the same distribution as $R_m=\frac{\sum_{r=1}^m U_rV_r}{(\sum_{r=1}^mU_r^2)^{1/2}(\sum_{r=1}^mV_r^2)^{1/2}},\qquad m=n-|S|-1,$ for $m$ independent copies $(U_r,V_r)$ of the standardized pair, whose correlation is $\rho=\rho_{ij\mid S}$ by [F1]. The hypothesis gives $m\ge3$. Their covariance block is positive definite by [F3], so the first residual sample column is nonzero almost surely, and conditional on that column the second has a density in $\mathbb R^m$. Let $x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(n)}\in\mathbb R^p$ be a sample, let $i\ne j$, and
let $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}\setminus\{i,j\}$. Let $\mathbf x_k\in\mathbb
R^n$ be the sample column for coordinate $k$, and let $\Pi_S$ be the orthogonal
projection onto the span of the all-ones vector and $\{\mathbf x_s:s\in S\}$.
When the sample covariance matrix of coordinates $\{i,j\}\cup S$ is positive
definite, define the residual columns
$$R_{i\mid S}=(I-\Pi_S)\mathbf x_i,\qquad R_{j\mid S}=(I-\Pi_S)\mathbf x_j.$$
The **sample partial correlation** is
$$\widehat\rho_{ij\mid S}=\frac{R_{i\mid S}^{T}R_{j\mid S}}{\|R_{i\mid S}\|_2\,\|R_{j\mid S}\|_2}.$$
For $-1<r<1$, the **Fisher transform** is
$g(r)=\frac12\log\frac{1+r}{1-r}$, and the sample Fisher statistic is
$Z_{ij\mid S}=g(\widehat\rho_{ij\mid S})$. For a test using multiplier
$\sqrt{n-|S|-3}$, require $n-|S|-3>0$ so that this factor is positive. Under independent samples
from a nondegenerate Gaussian law, the stated covariance block is positive
definite almost surely whenever $n-|S|-3>0$.

Assume AC. Let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_p)$ have a nondegenerate multivariate-normal
law with mean $\mu$ and positive-definite covariance matrix $\Sigma$. For
distinct indices $i,j$ and $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}\setminus\{i,j\}$, define
the conditional covariance block
$$
K_{ij\mid S}=\Sigma_{\{i,j\},\{i,j\}}-\Sigma_{\{i,j\},S}\Sigma_{S,S}^{-1}\Sigma_{S,\{i,j\}},
$$
with $K_{ij\mid\varnothing}=\Sigma_{\{i,j\},\{i,j\}}$. Whenever the diagonal
entries of this block are positive, the **partial correlation** is
$$
\rho_{ij\mid S}=\frac{(K_{ij\mid S})_{12}}{\sqrt{(K_{ij\mid S})_{11}(K_{ij\mid S})_{22}}}.
$$
The nondegenerate Gaussian case makes the conditioning covariance block
invertible; the following theorem proves that $K_{ij\mid S}$ is positive
definite, so this definition applies to every such $i,j,S$.

Assume AC. Let $X\sim N_p(\mu,\Sigma)$ be a nondegenerate multivariate-normal
vector, so $\Sigma$ is positive definite. For distinct $i,j$ and
$S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}\setminus\{i,j\}$, the block
$K_{ij\mid S}$ in the definition of Gaussian partial correlation is positive
definite, and
$$
\rho_{ij\mid S}=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\sigma(X_i)\perp\!\!\!\perp\sigma(X_j)\mid\sigma(X_S).
$$

Fix $0\le M<1$. There are constants $c_M>0$ and $C_M<\infty$ such that the
following holds. Let $X^{(1)},\ldots,X^{(n)}$ be independent observations from
a nondegenerate Gaussian law, and let $i,j,S$ be as in the definitions of
population and sample partial correlation. Suppose
$|\rho_{ij\mid S}|\le M$ and $n-|S|-3>0$. Then, for $0<t\le1$,
$$
\mathbb P\!\left(\left|g(\widehat\rho_{ij\mid S})-g(\rho_{ij\mid S})\right|>t\right)
\le C_M\exp\!\left(-c_M(n-|S|-1)t^2\right),
$$
where $g(r)=\tfrac12\log((1+r)/(1-r))$. The constants do not depend on
$i,j,S,n$ or the Gaussian mean and covariance beyond the bound $M$.

Assume AC and the causally sufficient perfect-oracle discovery regime for a
finite observed DAG $G$ and its full-joint law. Running the population PC
algorithm with any fixed vertex order returns exactly the skeleton of $G$,
records a d-separating set for every deleted pair, orients exactly the
unshielded colliders of $G$, and returns the CPDAG for the Markov-equivalence
class of $G$.

**Input:** A finite vertex set $V$, a perfect conditional-independence oracle
for a law in the causally sufficient discovery regime, and a fixed total order
of $V$. For every adjacent pair and conditioning set $S$ tested below, the
oracle returns whether $X_i$ and $X_j$ are conditionally independent given
$X_S$.

Assume AC. Let $(X_v)_{v\in V}$ be random elements in measurable spaces
whose joint law is generated, in a topological order of the finite DAG $G$,
by probability kernels $K_v(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v)},dx_v)$. For pairwise
disjoint $A,B,C\subseteq V$, if $C$ d-separates $A$ and $B$ in $G$, then
$$\sigma(X_A)\perp\!\!\!\perp\sigma(X_B)\mid\sigma(X_C).$$
This is the global Markov implication. Its converse is the separate
faithfulness condition in [[def-faithfulness-of-a-dag-model]].

Assume AC, and let a joint law $P$ on the measurable vertex variables of a
finite DAG $G$ be given. The law is **faithful to $G$** if, for every triple
of pairwise disjoint vertex sets $A,B,C$, the conditional independence
$$\sigma(X_A)\perp\!\!\!\perp\sigma(X_B)\mid\sigma(X_C)$$
implies that $C$ d-separates $A$ and $B$ in $G$. This is the converse of the
global Markov implication; faithfulness is a separate assumption on the
specified law, not a consequence of DAG factorization. No claim about Markov
equivalence, skeletons, or unshielded colliders is included. Here $X_A$ is
the finite random vector $(X_v)_{v\in A}$ with the finite-product
sigma-algebra; for $A=\varnothing$ it is the unique random element of the
empty-product singleton.

Let $G$ be a finite DAG on $V$. For distinct vertices $i,j\in V$, the pair
$\{i,j\}$ is an edge of the skeleton of $G$ if and only if there is no
$S\subseteq V\setminus\{i,j\}$ that d-separates $i$ and $j$ in $G$.

A **perfect conditional-independence oracle** for this regime accepts any
pairwise disjoint $A,B,S\subseteq V$ and returns “independent” exactly when
$\sigma(X_A)$ and $\sigma(X_B)$ are conditionally independent given
$\sigma(X_S)$. The **causally sufficient perfect-oracle regime** consists of
the finite observed DAG, its Markovian recursive model and full-joint law, the
faithfulness condition, and this exact oracle. No latent vertex is omitted
from the graph supplied to the oracle.
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

derivations.claim: Since $q_n=O(n^{1-b})$ with $b>0$, eventually $n-q_n-3>0$, so [F1] makes every sample statistic in the search defined almost surely. Since $c_n\le M<1$, take $t=c_n/4\le1$ in [F4]. For every tested triple $(i,j,S)$, the probability that $|g(\widehat\rho_{ij\mid S})-g(\rho_{ij\mid S})|>c_n/4$ is at most $C_M\exp(-c_M(n-|S|-1)c_n^2/16)$. For large $n$, $q_n/n\to0$ and $n-q_n-1\ge n/2$, so each such probability is at most $C_M\exp(-c'_M n c_n^2)$ for a constant $c'_M>0$.

There are at most $N_n=\binom{p_n}{2}\sum_{\ell=0}^{q_n}\binom{p_n-2}{\ell} \le p_n^2(q_n+1)p_n^{q_n}\le p_n^{q_n+3}$ distinct pair-and-set tests, since $q_n\le p_n-1$ and $q_n+1\le p_n$. A union bound, which requires no independence between tests, shows that the event $E_n$ on which every test of size at most $q_n$ has Fisher-transform error at most $c_n/4$ has failure probability at most $C_M\exp\!\left((q_n+3)\log p_n-c'_M n c_n^2\right).$ The assumptions imply $n c_n^2\ge C_0 n^{1-2d}$ eventually and $(q_n+3)\log p_n=O(n^{1-b}\log n)=o(n^{1-2d})$, because $2d<b$. Thus, after reducing the positive constant in the exponent, $\mathbb P(E_n^c)\le\exp(-C n^{1-2d})$ for all sufficiently large $n$.

On $E_n$, if $\rho_{ij\mid S}=0$, then [F1] gives $|g(\widehat\rho_{ij\mid S})|\le c_n/4$. By [F3], this is the population conditional-independence case. Hence $T_{ij\mid S}\le\sqrt n c_n/4<\sqrt n c_n/2$, so the test declares independence. If $\rho_{ij\mid S}\ne0$, then [F2] and the lower-bound hypothesis give $|\rho_{ij\mid S}|\ge c_n$, and $|g(\rho_{ij\mid S})|\ge|\rho_{ij\mid S}|$ because $|\operatorname{atanh}(r)|\ge|r|$ for $|r|<1$. Therefore $|g(\widehat\rho_{ij\mid S})|\ge3c_n/4$. Since $(n-|S|-3)/n\ge(n-q_n-3)/n\to1$, for all sufficiently large $n$ we have $\sqrt{(n-|S|-3)/n}>2/3$, so $T_{ij\mid S}>\sqrt n c_n/2$ and the test declares dependence. By [F3] these are exactly the dependent cases.

On $E_n$ the capped sample PC search makes the same decisions as the perfect-oracle algorithm at every level through $q_n$. True edges are never removed, because their one-edge paths prevent d-separation and [F7] makes every such test dependent. For each nonedge, [F8] supplies a separating parent set of size at most the true maximum degree $q_n$; its parent edges remain, so the algorithm tests and removes that nonedge no later than level $q_n$. Thus the sample search has the exact skeleton and separating sets on $E_n$, and its collider and R1–R3 orientations equal those of population PC. By [F5] its output is the CPDAG of $G_n$.

The only failure event is contained in $E_n^c$, whose probability has the bound from step 2.1. Step 4.1 identifies the output on $E_n$ as the CPDAG. This proves the stated consistency bound. The threshold uses $c_n$, so the theorem does not provide a data-driven choice of that parameter.

$\sqrt{n-|S|-3}$, require $n-|S|-3>0$ so that this factor is positive. Under independent samples
from a nondegenerate Gaussian law, the stated covariance block is positive
definite almost surely whenever $n-|S|-3>0$.

Assume AC. Let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_p)$ have a nondegenerate multivariate-normal
law with mean $\mu$ and positive-definite covariance matrix $\Sigma$. For
distinct indices $i,j$ and $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}\setminus\{i,j\}$, define
the conditional covariance block
$$
K_{ij\mid S}=\Sigma_{\{i,j\},\{i,j\}}-\Sigma_{\{i,j\},S}\Sigma_{S,S}^{-1}\Sigma_{S,\{i,j\}},
$$
with $K_{ij\mid\varnothing}=\Sigma_{\{i,j\},\{i,j\}}$. Whenever the diagonal
entries of this block are positive, the **partial correlation** is
$$
\rho_{ij\mid S}=\frac{(K_{ij\mid S})_{12}}{\sqrt{(K_{ij\mid S})_{11}(K_{ij\mid S})_{22}}}.
$$
The nondegenerate Gaussian case makes the conditioning covariance block
invertible; the following theorem proves that $K_{ij\mid S}$ is positive
definite, so this definition applies to every such $i,j,S$.

Assume AC. Let $X\sim N_p(\mu,\Sigma)$ be a nondegenerate multivariate-normal
vector, so $\Sigma$ is positive definite. For distinct $i,j$ and
$S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}\setminus\{i,j\}$, the block
$K_{ij\mid S}$ in the definition of Gaussian partial correlation is positive
definite, and
$$
\rho_{ij\mid S}=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\sigma(X_i)\perp\!\!\!\perp\sigma(X_j)\mid\sigma(X_S).
$$

Fix $0\le M<1$. There are constants $c_M>0$ and $C_M<\infty$ such that the
following holds. Let $X^{(1)},\ldots,X^{(n)}$ be independent observations from
a nondegenerate Gaussian law, and let $i,j,S$ be as in the definitions of
population and sample partial correlation. Suppose
$|\rho_{ij\mid S}|\le M$ and $n-|S|-3>0$. Then, for $0<t\le1$,
$$
\mathbb P\!\left(\left|g(\widehat\rho_{ij\mid S})-g(\rho_{ij\mid S})\right|>t\right)
\le C_M\exp\!\left(-c_M(n-|S|-1)t^2\right),
$$
where $g(r)=\tfrac12\log((1+r)/(1-r))$. The constants do not depend on
$i,j,S,n$ or the Gaussian mean and covariance beyond the bound $M$.

Assume AC and the causally sufficient perfect-oracle discovery regime for a
finite observed DAG $G$ and its full-joint law. Running the population PC
algorithm with any fixed vertex order returns exactly the skeleton of $G$,
records a d-separating set for every deleted pair, orients exactly the
unshielded colliders of $G$, and returns the CPDAG for the Markov-equivalence
class of $G$.

**Input:** A finite vertex set $V$, a perfect conditional-independence oracle
for a law in the causally sufficient discovery regime, and a fixed total order
of $V$. For every adjacent pair and conditioning set $S$ tested below, the
oracle returns whether $X_i$ and $X_j$ are conditionally independent given
$X_S$.

Assume AC. Let $(X_v)_{v\in V}$ be random elements in measurable spaces
whose joint law is generated, in a topological order of the finite DAG $G$,
by probability kernels $K_v(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v)},dx_v)$. For pairwise
disjoint $A,B,C\subseteq V$, if $C$ d-separates $A$ and $B$ in $G$, then
$$\sigma(X_A)\perp\!\!\!\perp\sigma(X_B)\mid\sigma(X_C).$$
This is the global Markov implication. Its converse is the separate
faithfulness condition in [[def-faithfulness-of-a-dag-model]].

Assume AC, and let a joint law $P$ on the measurable vertex variables of a
finite DAG $G$ be given. The law is **faithful to $G$** if, for every triple
of pairwise disjoint vertex sets $A,B,C$, the conditional independence
$$\sigma(X_A)\perp\!\!\!\perp\sigma(X_B)\mid\sigma(X_C)$$
implies that $C$ d-separates $A$ and $B$ in $G$. This is the converse of the
global Markov implication; faithfulness is a separate assumption on the
specified law, not a consequence of DAG factorization. No claim about Markov
equivalence, skeletons, or unshielded colliders is included. Here $X_A$ is
the finite random vector $(X_v)_{v\in A}$ with the finite-product
sigma-algebra; for $A=\varnothing$ it is the unique random element of the
empty-product singleton.

Let $G$ be a finite DAG on $V$. For distinct vertices $i,j\in V$, the pair
$\{i,j\}$ is an edge of the skeleton of $G$ if and only if there is no
$S\subseteq V\setminus\{i,j\}$ that d-separates $i$ and $j$ in $G$.

A **perfect conditional-independence oracle** for this regime accepts any
pairwise disjoint $A,B,S\subseteq V$ and returns “independent” exactly when
$\sigma(X_A)$ and $\sigma(X_B)$ are conditionally independent given
$\sigma(X_S)$. The **causally sufficient perfect-oracle regime** consists of
the finite observed DAG, its Markovian recursive model and full-joint law, the
faithfulness condition, and this exact oracle. No latent vertex is omitted
from the graph supplied to the oracle.
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

derivations.claim: Since $q_n=O(n^{1-b})$ with $b>0$, eventually $n-q_n-3>0$, so [F1] makes every sample statistic in the search defined almost surely. Since $c_n\le M<1$, take $t=c_n/4\le1$ in [F4]. For every tested triple $(i,j,S)$, the probability that $|g(\widehat\rho_{ij\mid S})-g(\rho_{ij\mid S})|>c_n/4$ is at most $C_M\exp(-c_M(n-|S|-1)c_n^2/16)$. For large $n$, $q_n/n\to0$ and $n-q_n-1\ge n/2$, so each such probability is at most $C_M\exp(-c'_M n c_n^2)$ for a constant $c'_M>0$.

There are at most $N_n=\binom{p_n}{2}\sum_{\ell=0}^{q_n}\binom{p_n-2}{\ell} \le p_n^2(q_n+1)p_n^{q_n}\le p_n^{q_n+3}$ distinct pair-and-set tests, since $q_n\le p_n-1$ and $q_n+1\le p_n$. A union bound, which requires no independence between tests, shows that the event $E_n$ on which every test of size at most $q_n$ has Fisher-transform error at most $c_n/4$ has failure probability at most $C_M\exp\!\left((q_n+3)\log p_n-c'_M n c_n^2\right).$ The assumptions imply $n c_n^2\ge C_0 n^{1-2d}$ eventually and $(q_n+3)\log p_n=O(n^{1-b}\log n)=o(n^{1-2d})$, because $2d<b$. Thus, after reducing the positive constant in the exponent, $\mathbb P(E_n^c)\le\exp(-C n^{1-2d})$ for all sufficiently large $n$.

On $E_n$, if $\rho_{ij\mid S}=0$, then [F1] gives $|g(\widehat\rho_{ij\mid S})|\le c_n/4$. By [F3], this is the population conditional-independence case. Hence $T_{ij\mid S}\le\sqrt n c_n/4<\sqrt n c_n/2$, so the test declares independence. If $\rho_{ij\mid S}\ne0$, then [F2] and the lower-bound hypothesis give $|\rho_{ij\mid S}|\ge c_n$, and $|g(\rho_{ij\mid S})|\ge|\rho_{ij\mid S}|$ because $|\operatorname{atanh}(r)|\ge|r|$ for $|r|<1$. Therefore $|g(\widehat\rho_{ij\mid S})|\ge3c_n/4$. Since $(n-|S|-3)/n\ge(n-q_n-3)/n\to1$, for all sufficiently large $n$ we have $\sqrt{(n-|S|-3)/n}>2/3$, so $T_{ij\mid S}>\sqrt n c_n/2$ and the test declares dependence. By [F3] these are exactly the dependent cases.

On $E_n$ the capped sample PC search makes the same decisions as the perfect-oracle algorithm at every level through $q_n$. True edges are never removed, because their one-edge paths prevent d-separation and [F7] makes every such test dependent. For each nonedge, [F8] supplies a separating parent set of size at most the true maximum degree $q_n$; its parent edges remain, so the algorithm tests and removes that nonedge no later than level $q_n$. Thus the sample search has the exact skeleton and separating sets on $E_n$, and its collider and R1–R3 orientations equal those of population PC. By [F5] its output is the CPDAG of $G_n$.

The only failure event is contained in $E_n^c$, whose probability has the bound from step 2.1. Step 4.1 identifies the output on $E_n$ as the CPDAG. This proves the stated consistency bound. The threshold uses $c_n$, so the theorem does not provide a data-driven choice of that parameter.
